title: The Mind as Bridge: What It Is For
reflection: Once a day, when a worry has you, take one slow breath and say inwardly: this is a thought, appearing in awareness. Notice the space it is happening in, and see whether the grip loosens even slightly.

questions.q: What are the two ways of knowing that Conversation 3.8 sets beside each other?
o: Difference-based knowing, with a gap between knower and known, and unity-based knowing, where the gap has closed.
Knowing by reading and knowing by listening, which differ only in the sense through which a thing is learned.
Quick knowing and slow knowing, which differ only in how much time a person takes before he is sure.
Knowing alone and knowing in company, which differ only in whether other people are there to help.
questions.e: At the same concert, one listener is frazzled and the music must push through clutter; the other is simply in it, and understanding arrives. The gap is the beat met all module. The first is the lower knowledge, nearer the surface; the second is the higher knowing, where the mind is in tune.

questions.q: James finds that some days he manages and monitors a lesson, and other days he disappears into it. On which do pupils learn more, and why?
o: The second, because he and the work have come into tune, and the gap that costs the energy has closed.
The first, because a teacher who watches himself and the clock is the one who keeps a lesson in order.
Neither, because what pupils learn depends wholly on the pupils and not at all on the teacher’s state.
Both the same, because the content of the lesson is what counts and the way it is given does not.
questions.e: James says there is no contest: the second. In the second the teaching just happens and does not even feel like effort. The practice this week is to find that second-listener state on purpose, setting down the monitoring for a few minutes and dropping into the teaching itself.
questions.c: The closed gap is where learning flows

questions.q: “The Upanishad line that the mind alone is the cause of both bondage and freedom says the mind is the problem and should be silenced.”
questions.e: The line does not say the mind is the problem. It says the mind is neutral, an instrument that can run in two modes. In one it manufactures the sense of separation; in the other it becomes clear and lets wholeness be seen. The path is not to destroy the mind but to retune it.
questions.c: The mind is neutral, to be retuned

questions.q: What does Swamiji mean by calling the mind a bridge?
o: It stands between the world of time, space and cause and the whole seen at once, and can turn either way.
It joins one person’s mind to another’s, so that thoughts can pass between them by way of the bridge.
It joins the past to the present, so that memories can be carried over into whatever is happening now.
It joins the body to the senses, so that the signals of the nerves may be sent to the brain and back.
questions.e: Turned one way, the bridge steps the vast awareness down into separate parts, which then look like the only reality. Turned the other way, it lets wholeness be recognised again, without ever losing the ability to come back and do the taxes. The enemy was never the bridge, only forgetting it can turn.
questions.c: The mind is a bridge between two worlds

questions.q: Sarah says the only stage of practice she has met is the slipping and returning, and she feels she is bad at it. What does Swamiji tell her?
o: The slipping and returning is the practice working: each return builds the bridge a step at a time.
She is right to be concerned, since a person who keeps slipping is not yet suited to meditation.
The slipping will stop if she tries harder, so she should simply put more force into holding on.
Practice is not meant to feel like work, so she should stop until the effort is gone of itself.
questions.e: The three stages are one process deepening: effortful holding, then an unbroken thread like oil poured from a jug, then moments when the gap is gone. Nobody starts on the far shore. What feels like failing is the early form of succeeding.
questions.c: Slipping and returning is the practice working

questions.q: “When the gap is gone in unity-based knowing, the mind has switched off and gone blank.”
questions.e: James hears blankness; Swamiji answers with a clear crystal. It is not switched off: it is so clear that it takes the form of whatever rests beside it, with no tint of its own. The mind goes transparent, not blank. It is mind with the fog taken out, and none of the light.
questions.c: The crystal goes transparent, not blank

questions.q: Sarah asks whether, having seen that the wave is the ocean, a person can still make dinner and worry about her children. What does Swamiji say?
o: Yes, and love them fiercely, without the constant ache of feeling cut off from everything and everyone.
No, since a person who has seen this has no further need of the ordinary world and its worries.
Yes, but only for a time, since in the end the ordinary world has to be left behind altogether.
No, since love for one’s own children is a form of attachment that has to be given up at this stage.
questions.e: The wave keeps waving. It just stops being terrified of the sea it is made of. Nothing was added; it recognised what was already true. You do not leave the ordinary world; you stop taking it for the whole.
questions.c: The wave keeps waving, without the terror

questions.q: Dr Watson asks a patient to take three slow breaths and notice that these are just thoughts. What has he done, in Swamiji’s account?
o: Shifted her from being lost in the content to noticing the awareness it appears in: the flicker loosens.
Solved the future she was afraid of, so that there is nothing left for her to worry about at all.
Silenced her thoughts for good, so that she will not be troubled by them again in any form.
Distracted her for a moment, so that the worry is replaced by a different and pleasanter thought.
questions.e: He has not silenced the thoughts or solved the future. The loosening is the bridge turning slightly toward the wider view: stepping back from the wave to notice the water. The same instrument that makes the symptom carries the recovery.
questions.c: One breath, one noticing: the bridge turns

questions.q: Kai asks whether machines doing so much thinking make inner work obsolete. What does Swamiji say?
o: The opposite: machines excel at difference-based knowing, so unity-based knowing is the human work.
Yes, in part, since a machine can do most of what the contemplative texts ask of a person.
No, since machines cannot read the contemplative texts or put any of the wise words together.
It makes no difference, since machines and people alike do the same kind of knowing in the end.
questions.e: A machine can imitate the second listener, with wise-sounding words, but that is still the first kind of knowing dressed in the language of the second. Direct recognition needs an I am present to do the recognising. It cannot be handed over, and the machines, by being so good at one mode, show us the other.
questions.c: Unity-based knowing is the distinctly human work

questions.q: Kai is asked to spend ten minutes with the night sky, a piece of music or a person he loves. What is he looking for?
o: The difference between thinking about it and simply being with it, as his own evidence.
A way to put into words what he sees, so that he can describe the sky or the music to the others.
A feeling of being small, which he is to hold on to, so that he does not think too highly of himself.
A fact about the sky or the music that he does not already know, so that he comes away with more.
questions.e: Kai is the sceptic, so the practice is an experiment: something that does not reduce to information, with the gap closed. The aim is not analysis or description but noticing that the difference is real and his.
questions.c: Notice the difference between thinking about and being with
